messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
At 22 years old, Miguel Martinez found himself trapped in the aftermath of a tragic accident that forever altered his life. As an HVAC technician, he had enjoyed the hands-on nature of his work, relishing the satisfaction of solving problems in various buildings. However, one fateful day, while working on a rooftop unit, he accidentally caused a serious injury to a co-worker, who fell and broke his leg severely. The sight of his colleague writhing in pain, coupled with the realization of his role in the incident, left Miguel grappling with a profound sense of guilt and despair. He couldn’t shake the feeling that he had failed to protect someone he considered a friend. Over time, this guilt morphed into a belief that he was an unreliable person, leading him to view his body as a traitor that had let him down at the most critical moment.

In the months following the accident, Miguel developed maladaptive strategies to cope with his overwhelming feelings. He began to avoid any dates or anniversaries related to the event, fearing that even a simple mention of the accident would plunge him back into the guilt and shame he felt. This avoidance extended to stressful situations in general; he would often decline social invitations or skip work if he sensed the day might be difficult, believing that staying away would protect him from feeling like a failure again. Yet, deep down, he recognized that this avoidance only reinforced his negative self-appraisal. He felt as though he was retreating from life, furthering the belief that he was unrecognizable and diminished from the person he once was.

Miguel's memories of the accident haunted him relentlessly. He often found himself trapped in an agonizing loop, replaying the events over and over in his mind, trying to make sense of how it could have happened. These memories felt alien, as if they belonged to someone else. The moment he thought about the incident, he would inexplicably catch a whiff of the metallic smell of the tools he used that day, instantly transporting him back to that rooftop and the horror of the accident. Unable to control the intrusive memories, Miguel experienced a heightened sense of threat. The silence in his apartment became deafening, triggering a fear that something dangerous might be lurking just out of sight, ready to pounce.

This constant threat perception further exacerbated Miguel's memory disturbances. Every time he was reminded of the accident, whether by a sound, a sight, or even an unremarkable silence, it would force the memory back into his consciousness. He had come to associate unexpected quiet with impending danger, fueling his anxiety and making his environment feel perilous. Consequently, he sought refuge in familiar places that felt safe, yet he realized that this self-imposed limitation on his life only deepened his belief that he was fragile and untrustworthy.

In grappling with these emotions, Miguel felt as if he were spiraling deeper into a cycle of self-reproach. His maladaptive strategies bred further negative appraisals, leaving him feeling trapped in a cycle he could not escape. The very actions he took to avoid stress and discomfort only served to heighten his feelings of guilt and inadequacy, creating an unending loop of fear and regret. He recognized that his life was shrinking around him, and the world felt increasingly dangerous.

Finally, after months of isolation and turmoil, Miguel reached a breaking point. He could no longer tolerate the weight of his guilt and fear. The thought of seeking help filled him with trepidation, yet he found himself hoping that perhaps, through therapy, he might learn to forgive himself and navigate the memories that felt so alien. He was terrified of what confronting his trauma might entail, yet he longed to reclaim the person he once was, to step back into life without the incessant shadow of the accident looming over him. It was this fragile hope that finally drove Miguel to seek professional help, yearning to understand how to reconcile his painful past with the possibility of a brighter future.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals influence or lead to memory disturbances.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not show that the perceived threat influences or causes memory disturbances.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette lacks a causal connection where maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not demonstrate that maladaptive strategies contribute to or exacerbate the sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time, this guilt morphed into a belief that he was an unreliable person, leading him to view his body as a traitor that had let him down at the most critical moment. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This belief that he was weak and inadequate made the memories of the accident more vivid, as if they were always waiting for him to revisit the moment of his failure, reinforcing his negative self-view. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The silence in his apartment became deafening, triggering a fear that something dangerous might be lurking just out of sight, ready to pounce. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This heightened sense of threat kept the memories of the accident close to the surface, as if they were a necessary reminder of the danger he felt was always present, forcing him to relive the event repeatedly. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He began to avoid any dates or anniversaries related to the event, fearing that even a simple mention of the accident would plunge him back into the guilt and shame he felt. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Yet, each time he avoided reminders of the incident, he felt a growing sense of fragility, convincing himself that he could not handle the emotional weight of the memories, which only deepened his negative self-appraisal. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Consequently, he sought refuge in familiar places that felt safe, yet he realized that this self-imposed limitation on his life only deepened his belief that he was fragile and untrustworthy. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
His constant avoidance left him with no evidence that the world outside was safe, reinforcing his perception of an ongoing threat that loomed just beyond his self-imposed barriers. 
<<<END>>>
